https://www.dw.com/en/unicef-1-in-5-yout.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5K1Xh A new survey by UNICEF found that one in five teenagers had been the target of online sexual abuse over the past year Image: Robin Utrecht/ROBIN UTRECHT/picture alliance Advertisement The internet is not a safe place for unsupervised children and young people — by now, that's common knowledge. Social media platforms are adept at tweaking their algorithms to ensure users of any age remain on their sites. To do that, they often disseminate content that can be dangerous and upsetting for young people. Studies regularly find a connection between what's known as doomscrolling and a higher risk of psychological problems in the young, including suicidal thoughts. And some of the latest trends in video creation on platforms like TikTok directly endanger the safety of users. In the United States, Meta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, recently opted to settle a case against it out of court. A number of US states had claimed that the two platforms harmed children. In the court case against Meta, held in Oakland, California, the corporation avoided a conviction by reaching a financial settlement with states Image: Vicki Behringer/REUTERS Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion (€14.7 billion) to the states involved and to limit teenagers' access to its platforms to just two hours a day. During the night, access will be completely blocked. A new survey by UNICEF , the UN agency for children, puts the spotlight on another danger that young people constantly face in the digital world: sexual assault , a threat experienced by one in five people between the ages of 12 and 17 over the past year. What are the key findings? The UNICEF report, which DW saw in advance of publication, explains how such attacks often happen. "It often begins without warning," the authors of the study wrote. "Conversation becomes coercion, and coercion becomes entrapment." The survey found that more than 15 million children had been exposed to unwanted sexual content. An estimated 9 million were pressured into sexual conversations or asked to share sexual images, while some 4 million had sexual images shared without their consent. The report's authors, however, warn that the true scale is likely far higher. "The report reveals a painful reality," said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. "These experiences cause profound emotional and mental distress. Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help." Often, the perpetrator of the assault puts pressure on a victim. The victims then feel ashamed and this makes it difficult to tell anybody about what has happened. Of those surveyed, 41% had never told anybody about their assault. Others said they had first confided in friends, siblings or their mothers. F ewer than 1% were reported to authorities. The stereotype many have of a complete stranger harassing young people online actually only applies in 16% of cases. Most perpetrators — 57% — are already known to their victims. They may be friends, family members or even romantic partners. In addition, 27% of respondents were not able to identify the people behind the profiles. When perpetrators are known, they include adults but also minors. In many cases, attacks take place in real life as well as online. The major social media platforms are also the main gateways for this kind of behavior. The UNICEF report says 60% of assaults come primarily from Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram (all of which are owned by Meta), followed by Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube . And 14% of respondents cited online gaming platforms as the location of an assault — gaming platforms usually have direct messaging channels. How was the data collected? The report polled around 21,000 young people in 21 countries, aged between 12 and 17, who regularly use the internet. Data from 12 countries — Ethiopia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Kenya, Malaysia, Mozambique, Namibia, the Philippines, Tanzania, Thailand, Uganda and Vietnam — had already been collected in 2020 and 2021 and analyzed in an earlier report. For this new report, additional data was collected in Armenia, Brazil, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Pakistan and Serbia. The surveys were also supplemented by longer interviews with 100 young people who had experienced abuse. Children and young people also come into contact with inappropriate content in the form of fakes created by generative AI, such as these images generated by Grok of the platform X Image: Leon Neal/Getty Images Europe, US surveys find similar results Researchers familiar with this issue would not be surprised by the scale of the problem. The 2020 EU Kids Online Survey, based on a poll conducted in 19 European countries, indicated that 22% of all participants had received sexually explicit messages online. In a Spanish study conducted in seven secondary schools in 2021 and 2022, 21% of female respondents said they were sexually harassed online "occasionally," while 5% said this happened "frequently." For male respondents in the Spanish study, the percentages were a few points lower. A similar survey conducted by the Pew Research Center in 2022 found that 17% of 13- to 17-year-olds in the US said they had been sent explicit images without their consent. The survey did not differentiate between sexually explicit content and other material that showed things like violence. Social media bans in Australia, UK, France The UNICEF report calls on governments, tech companies and other stakeholders to better protect children and young people in the digital world. Among the requests: Design more secure digital platforms, with stronger protection for the privacy of minors. Strengthen national regulations and criminal law, and close loopholes. Establish trustworthy reporting and support systems for young people. Coming just after Meta's out-of-court settlement in the US, the new UNICEF report will likely add fuel to the fire for those seeking to ban social media for young people, an ongoing debate in many countries. In December 2025, Australia became the first country in the world to introduce an age limit for social media in order to protect minors. There, anyone under 16 is prohibited from having an account on platforms like YouTube, X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat, a rule the platforms themselves are required to monitor. A similar age limit will come into effect in the UK in 2027, while France is the first EU country to have passed a law adopting an age limit — 15 years old — for social media users. However, it has since been blocked by France's top court, the Constitutional Council, which ruled it might infringe on freedom of expression and privacy. In June, a German commission proposed a tiered model. This would come with age limits, requirements for proof of age and strict rules requiring the cooperation of social media platforms. This article was originally written in German. Photograph: Martyna Adamska Poland Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban ‘AbortOmat’ in Warsaw offers novel way to challenge country’s restrictions and allow women swift, anonymous access Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent Sun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 05.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion. View image in fullscreen The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March last year by the Abortion Dream Team. Photograph: Martyna Adamska Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home. “And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind last week’s launch. “You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?” The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power. Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions. While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. View image in fullscreen Protests against the tightening of abortion laws, Oct 2020 in Warsaw. Photograph: Omar Marques/Getty Images The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.” The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.” But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.” While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska. It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.” Explore more on these topics Poland Abortion Europe Health Women news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://english.news.cn/europe/20260925/.text: Polish plan for EV hub reflects Europe's changing auto map The planned EV hub in Jaworzno in Silesia, southern Poland, will combine production, supplier development and research. KATOWICE, Poland, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Poland is looking to turn one of its old industrial heartlands into a new center for electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing, as the European auto industry shifts toward electrification, digital technologies and more localized supply chains. The planned EV hub in Jaworzno in Silesia, southern Poland, will combine production, supplier development and research. Discussions at this week's New Mobility Congress 2026 in Katowice point to an ambition that goes beyond a single assembly plant: retaining more of the technology, skills and industrial value created as Europe's automotive landscape changes. EUROPE'S EV SHIFT Europe's transition is gathering pace. The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) said 1.64 million battery-electric cars were registered in the EU in the first eight months of 2026, up 44.9 percent year-on-year. Their market share rose to 21.7 percent from 15.8 percent a year earlier. This market shift is being matched by policy. In July, the European Commission proposed raising electrification from about 23 percent of EU energy use today to 46 percent by 2040, with transport among the priority sectors. A 1.5-billion-euro (about 1.71 billion U.S. dollars) Battery Booster Facility launched in June is aimed at helping battery-cell production scale up within the European Economic Area. The issue is no longer simply how many research projects Europe can fund, said Olivier Silla, head of the Department for Sustainable Networks and Investments at the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA). "The challenge is not simply to pilot good ideas. It is to build value chains, infrastructure, skills and manufacturing capabilities in Europe," he said. WHY POLAND, WHY SILESIA Poland is entering the transition with a large manufacturing base but a relatively young EV market. Battery-electric cars made up about 5.1 percent of new-car registrations in the first eight months of 2026, far below the EU average. Nevertheless, the country is also firmly embedded in Europe's logistics network. Poland recorded 381 billion ton-kilometers of road freight transport in 2025, or 20.2 percent of the EU total, the highest share among member states, according to Eurostat. These strengths are concentrated in Silesia, home to a long-established automotive workforce and supplier base. Jaworzno's industrial zone lies near the A4 and S1 corridors and is connected by rail to the E30 route, placing it on freight routes serving Germany as well as the Czech Republic, Slovakia and other Central European markets. BEYOND ASSEMBLY The longer-term value of new EV investment will depend on how much expertise and industrial capability can be concentrated locally. Cyprian Gronkiewicz, CEO of ElectroMobility Poland, said a genuine automotive hub needs three things -- large-scale manufacturing, a local supplier base and R&D capacity. What matters, he said, is what remains once a model reaches the end of its production cycle -- engineering teams, suppliers and intellectual property. Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Digital Affairs Krzysztof Gawkowski placed talent at the center of the equation. "In the next phase of mobility, the advantage will belong to countries that are more digitalized, have stronger skills and can keep highly qualified people at home," he said. The Jaworzno plan therefore carries significance beyond one Polish industrial project. For Poland, the next step is to turn an established manufacturing base into a deeper EV ecosystem built around suppliers, engineering, research and technology, and to secure a larger role in Europe's evolving automotive value chain. ■ News In-depth Sports Business Culture World China Regions Asia & Pacific Europe Middle East North America South America Africa Organizations Services Weather Live & Work in China Doing Business Investment Visit China Study in China More Special Reports Photos Video Corrections About Us Contact Us Media Qiushi Journal Taiwan.cn Youth.cn GMW.cn CE.cn Ecns.cn China Daily CRI.cn China.org.cn People's Daily
